protocol.runner_fails_closed: a check the runner could not compute (None) counts as a failure -- this is the existing module's semantics and is NOT changed here
protocol.execution: one isolated child process per pool row (ThreadPoolExecutor driving subprocess.run), CPU-only
protocol.row_timeout_policy: a row whose PoseBusters call exceeds row_timeout_s is KILLED and recorded with status 'timeout'. A timeout is a CENSORING event, not a chemistry verdict: it counts as NOT pb_valid in the strict rate, and the counts block reports n_timeout and a completed-only rate so the censoring is visible.
protocol.row_timeout_rationale: MEASURED 2026-11-01: the three longest pool SMILES took 86.7 s / 60.5 s / 0.1 s on a single molecule-level check_posebusters call, and an in-process pool blocks indefinitely on such a row. The child-process cap is what makes a FULL-POOL run terminate.

limitations: PoseBusters has NO metal-coordination-sphere check. A % PB-Valid for this pool says NOTHING about whether the metal is coordinated correctly (oxidation state, coordination number, dative bonds, trans-effect). This metric is a MOLECULE-GEOMETRY check, not a coordination-chemistry check.

MMFF94 cannot parameterise most metal centres. The PoseBusters 'internal_energy' check then returns None (missing), and the runner fails CLOSED, so a metal-containing molecule is reported as PB-invalid for a force-field reason rather than a geometry reason. The per_check_missing_counts block quantifies this.

The pooled PB verdict is NOT dominated by 'bad 3D geometry' in the usual sense. Two check failures dominate and both are structural rather than geometry-quality failures: 'all_atoms_connected' (a multi-fragment row cannot pass it) and 'internal_energy' (missing, because neither MMFF94 nor UFF can parameterise the metal centre). Read the pooled rate together with counts.by_pool_fragment_count and counts.per_check_not_true_counts before interpreting it.

MEASURED 2026-11-01 (source_pool.composition): fraction_rows_with_a_metal_atom = 1.0 -- EVERY row of this pool carries a metal centre, so the force-field parameterisation shortfall above is not a corner case, it is the whole pool.

The pool carries IMPLICIT hydrogens; RDKit AddHs is applied inside the embedding step but the pool SMILES themselves have no explicit-H atoms. The frontier dataset has explicit hydrogens. This alone breaks the comparison. MEASURED 2026-11-01: source_pool.composition.n_rows_with_an_explicit_hydrogen_atom_in_the_smiles = 0 of 2112.

The pool is THREE epoch-wise decodes of ONE checkpoint (704 rows each, 6 seeds per epoch). It is not a training-set-distribution sampling, it carries no checkpoint-to-checkpoint variance, and it is 3x smaller than the frontier band's 10,000-15,000 draws.

The conformer ensemble is seeded (ETKDGv3 randomSeed = 42 in molmetal/validation/posebusters_runner.py), so the result is reproducible for a fixed RDKit/PoseBusters version pair but is not a seed-averaged statistic.

PoseBusters' 'mol' config evaluates ONE conformer per molecule (posebusters/config/mol.yml -> modules/distance_geometry.py reads mol.GetConformer()); the other embedded conformers are optimised but not judged. The conformer_sensitivity_probe block measures how often that choice changes the verdict.
Rows that fail to embed are counted and reported under BOTH denominators; they are not silently dropped.

A per-row wall-clock cap (protocol.row_timeout_s) kills any row whose PoseBusters call overruns it. A timeout is a CENSORING event, not a chemistry verdict: it counts as NOT pb_valid in the strict rate, and counts.n_timeout plus the completed-only rate expose the censoring. The rows that hit the cap are the pathological ETKDG geometries (MEASURED: the three longest pool SMILES took 86.7 s / 60.5 s / 0.1 s on one molecule-level call), so the censoring is NOT random with respect to molecule size.

2026-11-01 (additive): the censoring is MEASURED, not only asserted. The timeout_recheck block re-runs the timed-out rows under a longer per-row cap and reports what verdicts they would have produced, so the direction and size of the timeout bias is quantified rather than described.
